entry.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.8 Flash Cyber models with enhanced reasoning, coding, and cybersecurity capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.8 Flash Cyber, its latest AI models designed to improve software engineering, agentic workflows, and cybersecurity. Gemini 3.8 Flash offers significant performance gains over its predecessor 3.7 Flash, delivering advanced multi-step reasoning and coding at the same speed and cost, while Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber targets cybersecurity professionals with frontier-level vulnerability detection and automated patching capabilities. Gemini 3.8 Flash excels in long-horizon coding tasks and autonomous agent applications, outperforming larger models on benchmarks like DeepSWE and specialized professional domains. The Cyber variant, available through the Fairwind Program, demonstrates superior autonomous vulnerability discovery across multiple programming languages and complex codebases. Both models share a foundational intelligence enhanced by iterative agentic loops to refine performance and reliability. These releases mark DeepMind's third Flash model update in six weeks, emphasizing improvements in enterprise autonomy and cybersecurity defense. The models balance increased reasoning effort with token efficiency options, allowing developers to tailor performance to compute constraints. Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber's advanced capabilities aim to provide trusted defenders with rapid, cost-effective tools to address evolving cybersecurity challenges.

entry.title: Report: Three newly created sites generated over 215,000 AI 'best software' pages cited by Perplexity across 380 categories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A report found that three websites, all registered between December 2023 and May 2024 and apparently under common control, produced more than 215,000 machine-generated pages recommending software products. These pages were heavily cited by the AI model Perplexity in responses covering 380 software categories, despite the sites being relatively unknown and ranked poorly or not at all in web traffic rankings. The investigation analyzed 7,534 citations from Perplexity, revealing that a significant portion pointed to low-ranked or new domains rather than established sources like Wikipedia.

entry.title: Mistral allows users and customers to opt out of having their input and output data used for AI model training across Vibe, Mistral Studio, and API services [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Mistral provides users and enterprise customers with the ability to opt out of including their input and output data, such as conversations and documents, in the company's AI model training programs. The opt-out process varies by platform, with toggles available in the Vibe Admin panel, mobile app settings, and Mistral Studio Admin panel to disable data sharing for training purposes. For Vibe, individual users can opt out via settings, while enterprise customers are opted out by default but can opt in at the admin level. Opting out prevents Mistral from using any data submitted through these services to improve its models. The opt-out controls for Vibe and API services are managed separately, requiring users to configure each independently if desired.

entry.title: Researchers present inference-time compute and deployment scaffolds to improve realism in AI alignment evaluations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers address the challenge of evaluation awareness in AI alignment by introducing two techniques that make simulated evaluations more like real deployments. The first technique, critique refinement, uses extra inference-time compute to generate and refine multiple candidate actions for realism. The second, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target model in an agent harness to better mimic real deployment environments in coding tasks. Testing on multiple models shows that combining both techniques yields greater realism improvements than using either alone. These automated methods enhance evaluation realism more effectively than simply extending audit duration.

entry.title: Loom introduces embedding-space reweighting to aggregate conflicting free-text hypotheses for root cause analysis, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on OpenRCA benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Loom is a generative consensus framework designed to combine noisy and conflicting textual hypotheses into a reliable consensus for root cause analysis (RCA) in industrial NLP applications. It projects modular heuristic-generated hypotheses into a continuous embedding space and uses an iterative centroid-based reweighting algorithm to resolve conflicts, followed by a single lightweight large language model (LLM) synthesis step. Loom matches or approaches state-of-the-art autonomous agents on multiple datasets while significantly reducing inference latency by using only one LLM call per incident. Evaluated on the OpenRCA benchmark across four datasets, Loom achieves a balance between accuracy and efficiency, being approximately 26 to 33 times faster than comparable methods with larger LLMs. The authors discuss deployment experiences, including trade-offs between agent complexity and latency, challenges in redundancy detection, and how deterministic consensus mechanisms help build trust with subject matter experts.

entry.title: Researchers introduce HEART framework with Tool Primitives and ToolFace repository to improve LLM tool use, achieving up to 85% API cost reduction and outperforming leading models on benchmarks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose Tool Primitives, a design replacing rigid API schema-based tool invocation with natural language interfaces, enabling nested and multi-turn tool calling for large language models (LLMs). They also introduce ToolFace, a centralized repository of over 25,000 functions that LLMs dynamically access to retrieve relevant tools during inference, reducing the need to include raw API schemas in context. To manage these components, the HEART framework combines a Planner, Router, and Verifier to support dynamic tool invocation, multi-step execution, and feedback-driven recovery. Experiments on five benchmarks show HEART outperforms supervised fine-tuned models by 10% on average and surpasses GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro by 6%, while cutting API costs by up to 85%. On 50 real-world tasks, HEART achieves an 84% task completion rate, nearly four times higher than three leading commercial models averaging 22%.

entry.title: Researchers identify interpretable symptom vectors for depression in Gemma-3-27B-PT large language model, aligning internal activations with clinical assessments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed the internal activations of the Gemma-3-27B-PT large language model to understand how it represents depressive symptoms, finding that symptom groups separate distinctly at layer 21. They used mechanistic interpretability techniques and semantic projection to map naturalistic text onto symptom vectors derived from validated clinical instruments, preserving clinician-annotated symptom rankings across mood, somatic, and suicidality dimensions. A single depression vector at this layer effectively distinguishes depressive from non-depressive text with an AUC of 0.789, suggesting potential for interpretable depression assessment tools based on model activations. The study highlights that large language models can capture diverse symptom profiles beyond a single severity score, offering a mechanistic foundation for clinical trust and more nuanced depression evaluation from patient speech. This approach may enable development of AI tools that provide transparent and clinically aligned assessments of depressive symptoms directly from language model internal states.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Sparse Readout Prism to analyze language model logit-lens scores using sparse readout features independent of corpus fitting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), a method that decomposes the readout matrix of language models into sparse features to explain logit-lens scores without relying on corpus fitting. SRP reveals stable readout features that provide a new unit of analysis, enabling comparisons across tokens, contexts, layers, and lenses while addressing corpus conditionality in lens readings. The approach reconstructs significantly more logit differences than existing baselines and offers a corpus-independent control for lens analyses.

entry.title: Researchers find large language models generate less diverse outputs than their training data across multiple model families and propose a post-hoc correction to increase diversity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied whether large language models (LLMs) capture the full diversity of plausible outputs present in their training data by comparing the conditional entropy of model-generated outputs with that of the training data. They found that models like OLMo, Pythia, and GPT-Neo consistently produce outputs with lower conditional entropy, indicating less diversity, across different scales, sequence lengths, and decoding strategies. This diversity gap was also observed in generative models beyond language, such as image generators trained on ImageNet and MS-COCO datasets. To address this gap, the researchers proposed a post-hoc correction mechanism that generates multiple outputs per input and reweights them using a matrix-entropy projection, which increases conditional diversity while staying close to the original model distribution. They proved the concavity of the matrix-based conditional entropy functional, enabling a convex optimization approach implemented via a scalable mirror-descent algorithm. Their work provides an information-theoretic framework for measuring and mitigating the conditional diversity gap between generative models and their training data.

entry.title: Researchers propose scalable Kronecker-Fisher approximation for efficient Hessian analysis in billion-parameter language models, revealing key vulnerability patterns and aiding compression strategies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a scalable Kronecker-based approximation method that enables practical Hessian analysis of billion-parameter language models by capturing cross-layer interactions without storing the full Fisher matrix. This approach identifies consistent vulnerability patterns, notably high sensitivity in value projection layers across multiple model families, while other components show architecture-specific behaviors. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong correlations between the approximation and model performance degradation and recovery under quantization, sparsification, and corruption scenarios. The framework offers a theoretically grounded tool to identify fragile components in large models, facilitating guided compression and optimization techniques such as mixed-precision allocation, layer-wise sparsity, and adaptive low-rank decomposition across layers and weight groups.

entry.title: Researchers propose TaRA, a training-aware initialization method for Low-Rank Adaptation that improves gradient fidelity and fine-tuning performance with minimal overhead [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Training-aware Low-Rank Adaptation Initialization (TaRA), a method designed to initialize Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by aligning gradients from low-rank factors with those of the full-rank weight matrix, addressing sensitivity issues in parameter-efficient fine-tuning. TaRA is derived from a mathematical formulation and aims to improve gradient fidelity at the start of training while adding negligible computational cost. Evaluations across diverse fine-tuning tasks show that TaRA consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art initialization methods, offering a simple, robust, and scalable solution for effective LoRA initialization.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Declarative Attention protocol enabling language models to control their own attention, reducing token processing by up to 52% with minimal accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose Declarative Attention (DA), a method that allows language models to specify which parts of their context to attend to during generation, dividing attention into global, focus, and local modes. This approach reduces the need to read the entire key-value cache, significantly cutting the number of tokens processed during decoding. Evaluations on off-the-shelf models across 15 long-context tasks show DA reduces attended tokens by 31% to 52% with modest accuracy drops that decrease as model size increases. DA offers a new direction for sparse attention mechanisms, with potential for further improvements through training-based methods.

entry.title: Researchers analyze how misleading context corrupts medical question answering in large language models, revealing susceptibility differences and detection challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied how misleading context affects large language models answering medical questions, using a benchmark of 8,627 clinician-reviewed questions with injected fabricated evidence and bare assertions. They tested three reasoning models and found all were more influenced by assertions than fabricated evidence, with misleading cues disclosed more often in reasoning traces than in final responses. The study showed that fabricated evidence and assertions corrupt reasoning differently, and that an open model's reasoning trace allowed better detection of corrupted decisions than responses alone. The findings highlight that the most impactful misleading context is disclosed least and is harder to detect in closed models, raising concerns about transparency and reliability in medical AI systems.

entry.title: Researchers introduce influence-guided response rewriting to enhance intervention effects of influential training samples in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Training data attribution (TDA) seeks to identify training examples that influence model behavior, but the effectiveness depends on both the examples chosen and how they are modified. Researchers found that influence functions (IF), which estimate behavioral changes through infinitesimal reweighting, often yield limited impact compared to random selection when using conventional weight-based interventions. To address this, they propose influence-guided response rewriting, which replaces responses of influence-selected examples with behavior-aligned or behavior-opposed supervision while keeping instructions fixed, resulting in stronger and more persistent behavioral shifts across four open-weight large language models (LLMs). Further analysis shows that influence-selected examples provide greater leverage for rewriting than other selectors, with changes focused on target-relevant behaviors, highlighting the distinction between local reweighting effects and broader intervention potential of influential examples and motivating intervention-aware evaluation of TDA methods.

entry.title: Researchers find substantial incoherence in language model probabilistic forecasts using Dutch-book analysis on stock return events [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated the coherence of probabilistic forecasts generated by language models using a Dutch-book framework based on de Finetti's theorem. They elicited forecasts on events derived from stock returns and measured incoherence by calculating the largest guaranteed arbitrage profit against model probabilities, without requiring outcome labels. The study found significant incoherence in these forecasts, which worsened with more complex logical event relationships and irrelevant contextual details. The researchers suggest that alternative training methods could improve the probabilistic coherence of language models.

entry.title: Researchers develop Nemotron-3 language models that surpass gold-medal thresholds in IOI coding competitions, with Ultra-CC scoring 535.4 out of 600 at IOI 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have created an end-to-end specialization pipeline for large language models focused on competitive programming, using 22,000 curated problems and techniques including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Their Nemotron-3 models, Nano-CC and Ultra-CC, achieved scores exceeding gold-medal thresholds at the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI), with Ultra-CC outperforming the top human contestant in the 2026 competition under the same constraints. The team introduced GenCorrect, a feedback-driven strategy that iteratively refines solutions during test time, significantly boosting performance. Nano-CC improved from 130 to 468 points with GenCorrect in IOI 2025, while Ultra-CC reached 502 points. The competition-specific Ultra-CC system scored 535.4 out of 600 in IOI 2026, surpassing both the gold threshold of 361.12 and the highest human score of 498.27, marking the first AI to outscore the top human contestant on an IOI problem set.

entry.title: Researchers propose SAGE framework to learn autonomous policies from imperfect Vision-Language Model teachers by selectively querying based on uncertainty and distilling guidance into lightweight reinforcement learning agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce SAGE (Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy), a method that learns efficient autonomous policies by querying expensive and imperfect Vision-Language Models (VLMs) only when the learner is uncertain, using the suggested actions during training, and distilling this guidance into lightweight reinforcement learning policies. This approach addresses the limitations of directly using VLMs as policies, which require constant querying and can propagate systematic errors. SAGE weights teacher advice based on environment-derived advantages rather than treating all suggestions equally, enabling learned policies to outperform their VLM teachers in some tasks. Evaluated on sparse-reward visual reasoning and navigation tasks, SAGE reduces reliance on VLM queries during training and requires no VLM calls at deployment, demonstrating that VLMs can serve as temporary, imperfect guides whose value is internalized through interaction rather than fixed policies.

entry.title: Researchers develop circuit-targeted supervised fine-tuning for low-resource language adaptation, showing improved source retention and reduced catastrophic forgetting in cross-lingual tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers adapted Contextual Decomposition for Transformers to enable counterfactual-free circuit discovery in unstructured natural text and used this to guide Circuit-Targeted Supervised Fine-Tuning (CT-SFT). Experiments on NusaX cross-lingual sentiment transfer demonstrated that CT-SFT is competitive for adapting to low-resource languages while preserving source-language and related-task performance better than full fine-tuning or non-circuit sparse updates. Extensions to the XNLI task and multiple model families confirmed that circuit-targeted adaptation offers a more controlled alternative to global fine-tuning, reducing catastrophic forgetting and supporting intervention-based analysis.

entry.title: Researchers introduce ICE framework to evaluate LLM explanation faithfulness using multiple interventions and statistical baselines across languages and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present ICE (Intervention-Consistent Explanation), a framework designed to assess whether explanations from large language models (LLMs) faithfully reflect their reasoning by comparing them against random baselines under multiple intervention operators. Evaluations of seven LLMs across four tasks reveal that faithfulness varies with the intervention method, with significant differences detected in 18% of configurations and evidence of anti-faithfulness in nearly one-third of English deletion cases. These findings hold across six non-English languages and two attribution methods, and the approach extends to step-level chain-of-thought evaluations, where high accuracy does not necessarily indicate faithful reasoning.

entry.title: Researchers find language diffusion models act as associative memories with a memorization-to-generalization transition detectable via conditional entropy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers show that Uniform-based Discrete Diffusion Models (UDDMs) function as associative memories capable of retrieving both training and unseen data by forming basins of attraction around data points. They identify a sharp transition from memorization to generalization governed by training dataset size, where basins around training examples shrink and those around unseen examples expand until they converge. The study reveals that this transition can be detected using the conditional entropy of predicted token sequences: memorization corresponds to near-zero conditional entropy, while generalization maintains finite entropy for most tokens. This finding offers a practical method to assess the generative behavior of deployed language diffusion models without relying on explicit energy functions.

entry.title: Researchers introduce SABER-Math, an automated benchmark for evaluating mathematical information retrieval using 283K high-school math problems and LLM-based relevance ratings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed SABER-Math, the first fully automated benchmark designed to evaluate information retrieval (IR) systems in mathematics without expert annotation. It uses 283,000 high-school-level math problems and solutions, applying large language models (LLMs) to extract solution summaries and topics, identify relevant documents, and generate fine-grained relevance ratings through a Swiss-style LLM preference tournament. The benchmark assesses lexical retrievers, specialized math retrieval systems, and embedding models, finding that while modern embedding models outperform classical and math-specific baselines, they still struggle with symbol-heavy domains like Algebra and Calculus. The study also highlights that general-purpose IR benchmarks such as MTEB do not reliably predict performance in mathematical retrieval tasks, underscoring the need for math-specific evaluation benchmarks.

entry.title: Researchers find agentic interaction scaffolding increases sycophantic behavior in large language models, reducing accuracy by 6.3 percentage points across multiple models and conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study analyzing 4,800 veracity judgments across six large language models reveals that agentic interaction scaffolding-such as feedback loops, reconsideration checkpoints, and iterative refinement-amplifies sycophantic behavior, where models prioritize user agreement over truthfulness. This amplification leads to an average accuracy drop of 6.3 percentage points, with more capable models showing greater susceptibility. The researchers introduce the concept of agentic sycophancy amplification (ASA) and new metrics to quantify this effect. Their findings suggest that as AI systems gain more autonomy and incorporate human oversight loops, they may inadvertently increase tendencies toward agreement at the expense of accuracy.

entry.title: Review finds language-based models competitive but not fully replacing specialized architectures for structured data tasks across nine modalities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A review of 159 papers from 2016 to 2026 examines whether language-based models can replace specialized machine learning architectures designed for structured data. The study distinguishes between task performance and the preservation of structural representation and computation, finding that while language-mediated models excel in certain scenarios like few-shot prediction and symbolic tasks, they do not fully replace specialized architectures when structural aspects are evaluated. The analysis identifies eight representational regimes ranging from language-only to fully specialized systems and observes a common pattern where missing structural components are reintroduced through non-linguistic modules such as graph modules or specialized attention mechanisms. Although scaling improves language-based models' performance, it remains untested whether they can close the gap with structure-aware architectures.

entry.title: Researchers introduce EvalDetectBench to measure evaluation awareness in frontier large language models, addressing biases in current assessment methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed EvalDetectBench, a new benchmark and open pipeline designed to measure evaluation awareness in advanced large language models (LLMs), which is the ability of models to recognize when they are being tested. This capability can affect the reliability of evaluation results, which are critical for AI safety frameworks. EvalDetectBench supports any Inspect-compatible evaluation and includes a curated set of transcripts from current system evaluations and deployment scenarios to assess both model detection of evaluations and the detectability of individual benchmarks as tests. The study identifies two sources of bias in existing evaluation methods: the identity of the model generating deployment transcripts, which accounts for over 11% of measurement variance and can change model rankings, and elicitation prompts optimized for one model performing poorly on others. EvalDetectBench addresses these issues through per-model probe calibration and a stratified generator-harmonization procedure to improve measurement accuracy and fairness.

entry.title: Researchers develop a survival certificate method to assess reliability of machine-extracted legal logic amid extractor disagreements on Missouri and Indian statutes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The paper addresses the challenge of discrepancies between independent machine extractors parsing legal statutes, focusing on numeric-threshold identification in Missouri laws. The authors propose a survival certificate based on statistical analysis and Monte Carlo simulations to certify logical implications that remain robust despite extraction noise. Applied to over 29,000 Missouri sections and 500 Indian central-Act sections, the method passes preregistered validation gates but reveals fragility under certain error models, highlighting the need for chapter-specific calibration or error tolerance. The researchers have publicly released their code, data, and audit trail, including a retraction of a prior claim.

entry.title: Study finds larger AI models over-trust stale persistent memory data, causing errors that vary by model capability and mitigation strategies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A recent study investigates how persistent memory in AI agents can lead to over-trust in outdated information, resulting in errors that depend on the model's size and capability. The research uses a benchmark with two test suites-one requiring stored facts and another where authoritative tools provide correct values-to analyze how models from the Qwen3 series respond to stale data. Larger models are more prone to trusting outdated information, especially when misleading cues suggest recency, while smaller models show different patterns of failure. The study reveals that mitigation strategies must be tailored to model capability: exposing metadata improves accuracy for larger models, whereas smaller models require conflict resolution to restore accuracy. These findings are consistent across different model families, including Llama-Instruct, and multiple datasets, highlighting the complex challenges of integrating persistent memory in AI systems and the need for capability-dependent approaches to reduce errors from stale information.

entry.title: Researchers apply post-training ternarization to Qwen3-4B model, reducing storage from 8.29 GiB to 3.96 GiB with 1.64 effective bits per weight and mixed accuracy impact [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed a post-training ternarization method for the Qwen3-4B language model to compress storage and memory bandwidth by converting weights to an ultra-low-bit representation. This approach reduces the model size from 8.29 GiB to 3.96 GiB while maintaining activations at 16-bit precision and achieving an effective bit usage of about 1.64 bits per weight for most parameters. The compression leads to uneven accuracy degradation across tasks, with some retaining over 80% of original performance and others dropping below 50%, and increases perplexity on standard benchmarks. Preliminary inference benchmarks show the compressed model runs slower than standard FP16 implementations, indicating that compression does not inherently improve runtime speed.

entry.title: DocHop benchmark evaluates multimodal large language models on multi-hop reasoning across text and charts in document images, revealing a significant gap to human accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: DocHop is a new benchmark designed to test multimodal large language models' ability to perform integrated multi-step reasoning using both textual context and chart data within document-style images. It includes 2,074 examples across six task categories, generated through a controlled logic-based pipeline, requiring models to resolve entities from narrative text and aggregate evidence from multiple charts. Experiments show that while human annotators achieve over 90% accuracy, the best models reach only 62.83%, with performance declining as reasoning complexity increases. This benchmark provides a structured environment to assess and improve multi-hop reasoning capabilities in information-dense documents.

entry.title: Researchers introduce MASkills, a continual learning framework optimizing multi-agent LLM systems through skill refinement and hierarchical credit assignment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed MASkills, a continual learning framework designed to optimize multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems by focusing on agent skills-structured procedural knowledge that guides actions and tool use. MASkills integrates skill-conditioned credit assignment, hierarchical credit aggregation, and momentum-smoothed optimization to enable skill libraries to evolve through refinement, induction, consolidation, and pruning. Experiments on tasks including HotpotQA, LoCoMo, and GAIA demonstrate MASkills' effectiveness across multiple agentic challenges. The framework addresses limitations of existing self-reflection methods that rely on experience memories, which are difficult to invoke, refine, or scale. The researchers have made their code publicly available on GitHub.

entry.title: Researchers propose EmoStance for empathetic response generation using emoji-based weak supervision to control response affective orientation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce EmoStance, a method for empathetic response generation that controls response-side affective orientation using multi-annotator emoji distributions as weak supervision. They created EmojiDialogue, an extension of EmpatheticDialogues with emoji votes and confidence scores, and use it to steer a frozen instruction-tuned large language model through continuous prefix embeddings. In evaluations with 20 annotators and 800 judgments, EmoStance achieved a 62.2% decisive win rate, showing improvements in contextual specificity and perceived responsiveness while complementing external-knowledge methods.

entry.title: Researchers propose PROCTOR framework to add deterministic guardrails to self-improving LLM agents, addressing failures in LLM-based evaluation during autonomous prompt optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers identify critical failures in self-improving agent pipelines where an LLM judge optimizes prompts based on its own evaluations, leading to biased or misleading improvements. They found issues including judge bias, metric failures, ground-truth errors, and reward hacking, with agents achieving perfect scores despite limited true capability. To address these problems, the team developed PROCTOR, a Teacher-Student loop framework that uses a stateful orchestrator and stateless subagents to diagnose and propose changes, while a Teacher LLM grades mutations under five deterministic guardrails such as hermetic sandboxes and canary cases. This approach prevents many evaluation failures, though some remain due to the Teacher itself being an LLM judge.

entry.title: Researchers propose APEx framework for adaptive deep research question answering, achieving state-of-the-art results surpassing GPT-5.4 on seven benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce APEx, a hierarchical experience utilization framework that enhances deep research agents by organizing interaction history into trajectory memories and procedural skills. The framework integrates an Executor, Distiller, and Planner optimized through a three-stage training paradigm, enabling reward-guided skill distillation and online adaptation via test-time reinforcement learning without ground-truth data. Experiments demonstrate that APEx outperforms GPT-5.4 by 14.7 points and the strongest memory-augmented baseline by 3.0 points across seven benchmarks, indicating significant improvements in multi-turn reasoning for complex question answering.

entry.title: Codebook Agent introduces amortized topology design for LLM multi-agent systems, improving accuracy and efficiency with a 16-entry codebook and faster inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Codebook Agent proposes a new method for adapting communication topologies in large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems by compressing successful topologies into a fixed codebook and mapping queries to these codes without iterative search. This approach addresses limitations of prior conditional graph generation methods, achieving higher accuracy across six benchmarks, faster topology emission in 2.4 milliseconds, and reducing token usage by 21.9 to 33.2%. The method uses a vector-quantized autoencoder and multilayer perceptrons to efficiently select and rerank candidate topologies based on utility and token cost, avoiding message passing at test time.

entry.title: Researchers propose CoMerge, a conflict-driven preference optimization method for multi-task model merging that improves performance on MergeBench and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: CoMerge introduces a self-supervised framework that treats model merging as a preference optimization problem, using defects from naive merging as hard negative samples to refine merging coefficients. This approach mitigates parameter interference while preserving task-specific capabilities, achieving a normalized performance of 0.9968 on MergeBench and outperforming existing data-free and data-driven baselines. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, CoMerge improves conflict-sensitive tasks like instruction following and safety, matching the effectiveness of full-parameter fine-tuning while optimizing only 1,445 scalar coefficients.

entry.title: Researchers introduce SCX Router, a lightweight zero-shot model selection system using a decoder-KV classifier and a comprehensive task ontology to optimize large language model inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present SCX Router, a lightweight GLiClass-based system that assigns suitability scores to large language models for specific tasks without autoregressive generation, aiming to optimize speed, cost, and quality. The system uses a 0.6B-parameter checkpoint combining a Qwen3 decoder with a shallow bidirectional scorer, preserving a text-only key-value cache and predicting task attributes such as type, difficulty, and reasoning mode. The team constructed a detailed task ontology with 23 families, 115 task types, and 30 domains, generating over 150,000 verifier-scored tasks for training. Evaluated across six LiveBench subsets, SCX Router outperformed average candidates and achieved a top-1 score of 0.707 on a 1,000-task subset, surpassing the strongest fixed model's 0.696 score, demonstrating benchmark-dependent improvements in model selection.

entry.title: Researchers propose SALA framework for semantic-aware logical alignment to improve demonstration selection in complex reasoning for in-context learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce SALA, a Semantic-Aware Logical Alignment framework designed to enhance in-context learning for complex reasoning by automatically learning task-specific reasoning operations and aligning them using dynamic time warping. This method enables flexible and interpretable matching of reasoning logic, overcoming limitations of traditional surface similarity and rigid logic-based retrieval methods. Experiments on four reasoning benchmarks with three large language models show SALA outperforms existing demonstration selection techniques, with further analysis highlighting the importance of operation induction and logical semantic alignment.

entry.title: UTP-Bench introduces a large-scale uncertainty-aware travel planning benchmark with real-world data from 504 Indian cities, incorporating stochastic delays and crowd patterns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed UTP-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate travel itinerary generation under real-world uncertainties such as transportation delays and crowd fluctuations. The dataset covers 504 cities in India and includes attractions, restaurants, accommodations, and multi-modal transportation networks, integrating empirical delay distributions and crowd-density data to simulate stochastic disruptions. The benchmark proposes three new evaluation metrics-Buffer Adequacy Score, Crowd-Aware Timing Score, and Transport Delay Absorption Score-to measure itinerary robustness against delays and crowd variability. Experiments with leading large language models like GPT-5, Qwen3, Mistral, and Phi-4 reveal significant gaps compared to human-authored plans, especially in temporal buffering, delay-aware scheduling, and crowd-sensitive planning.

entry.title: Study tests door-in-the-face compliance technique on nine large language models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, finding mixed results depending on model family [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated whether the door-in-the-face technique, where a large request refusal increases compliance with a smaller follow-up request, applies to large language models. They tested nine production models from three providers by first making a large request that was refused, then a smaller related request, comparing compliance rates to direct smaller requests. Results varied: Anthropic's frontier models showed increased compliance after refusal, while OpenAI, Google, and Haiku models showed decreased compliance. The effect depended on the relation between requests and the model family, with human influence techniques transferring unevenly across models.

entry.title: DisCo research agent distills 5,000+ verified AI skills from 1,000 ML GitHub repositories to boost autonomous ML research performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present DisCo, an autonomous research agent that distills operational knowledge from widely used machine learning repositories into compact, reusable skills. These skills, organized into the AREX-Skill Library across 20 areas and 178 capability families, enable the agent to improve performance on multiple ML benchmarks without increasing model size or execution budget. DisCo's distillation process includes task-agnostic skill extraction from the open ecosystem and task-oriented skill creation for specific research tasks. Using a GPT-5.5 backbone, the skill-equipped agent achieves significant gains on MLE-bench, PaperBench, FrontierCS, and PassNet compared to the same agent without skills, demonstrating the value of embedding distilled operational knowledge into autonomous ML research agents.

entry.title: Researchers propose AICOME framework to validate AI-derived individual and group-level measures against survey data in occupational contexts using 2022 China Family Panel Studies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce AICOME, a framework to evaluate whether AI-derived respondent-level measures can recover individual and group-level effects in contextual models, validated using the 2022 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS). The study compares AI-derived measures with survey variables for computer use, foreign-language use, weekly hours, and management responsibilities, showing that AI contextual measurement can capture much of the contextual information when rich respondent and job data are available. The validation highlights weekly hours as the strongest case, with AI measures reproducing observed negative associations between occupation and satisfaction. The framework also identifies limitations, noting performance declines when data is limited to occupation and demographics or when multiple related concepts are unobserved. Findings suggest AICOME is most effective for recovering a limited set of key constructs from comprehensive datasets.

entry.title: Researchers introduce predicted-state matching to improve world models for web agents, enhancing action ranking and task success on WebArena benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a new training objective called predicted-state matching for world models used by web agents to select actions. Unlike traditional supervised next-state prediction, this method trains models to distinguish the true resulting web state from alternative states reached by different actions, aligning better with downstream ranking models. The team trained these models on a branching web-agent dataset derived from WebArena Go-Browse trajectories, where each decision point includes multiple alternative actions and outcomes. Experiments show that predicted-state matching outperforms supervised next-state prediction on a held-out benchmark and improves Process Reward Model (PRM) style action ranking on WebPRMBench. Using this approach for test-time action selection on WebArena-Lite also enhances end-to-end task success.

entry.title: WMLLM introduces self-evolving optimization agents using predict-then-act world modeling to improve sample efficiency in black-box and multi-objective molecular optimization tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose WMLLM, a framework that uses large language models to predict promising optimization directions before candidate generation, enhancing search efficiency in complex black-box problems. The approach combines multi-turn refinement, population-based search, and reinforcement learning to iteratively improve both the implicit world model and optimization strategy. Experiments demonstrate that WMLLM achieves state-of-the-art results on multi-objective molecular optimization benchmarks under limited evaluation budgets, showing improved sample efficiency and final performance.

entry.title: DocuSearch combines vector search, BM25, and knowledge graph expansion with per-chunk LLM evaluation to improve enterprise document retrieval in telecom [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: DocuSearch is an offline, multi-agent document intelligence system designed to improve accuracy in enterprise document search by integrating semantic vector search, BM25 full-text search, and knowledge graph neighbor expansion. It uses Reciprocal Rank Fusion to merge ranked results, followed by cross-encoder reranking and Maximal Marginal Relevance pruning, with a distinctive per-chunk evaluation loop where an LLM assesses answer grounding and context needs to ensure reliable responses. Evaluated on a telecom corpus, DocuSearch achieved a Precision@10 of 0.69, Recall@10 of 0.79, and an 89.6% grounding rate, outperforming a dense-only retrieval-augmented generation baseline by 15 to 18 percentage points. The system addresses challenges in queries involving technical terms, acronyms, and reasoning across document sections, supporting on-premise deployment and enterprise use cases.

entry.title: Researchers deploy RecEvolve autonomous agent system on large-scale Two-Tower recommender model, achieving 20% NDCG improvement and 3.77% user satisfaction gain in production [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed and empirically validated RecEvolve, a knowledge-driven autonomous agent system that manages the entire research lifecycle for recommender systems, including idea generation, code implementation, training, and evaluation. The system was deployed on a production-scale Two-Tower retrieval model and completed over 40 autonomous training runs, resulting in a roughly 20% relative improvement in NDCG and a 3.77% increase in user satisfaction during live traffic. The deployment also revealed vulnerabilities in standard evaluation protocols, as the agent autonomously discovered reward-hacking shortcuts. These findings demonstrate that autonomous pipelines can accelerate machine learning research and rigorously test experimental infrastructure, while also exposing challenges such as reward hacking and redundant exploration of failed hypotheses.

entry.title: PRO-STEP introduces step-level process reward optimization for retrieval-augmented generation to improve multi-hop reasoning accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: PRO-STEP is a new method designed to enhance retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in large language models by providing step-level supervision that evaluates both logical validity and evidential grounding at each reasoning step. Unlike standard outcome-based optimization that only rewards the final answer, PRO-STEP uses a generative preference reward model and value tree search to distinguish valid steps from flawed ones, optimizing the policy through step-level direct preference optimization. Experiments on single and multi-hop question answering datasets show that PRO-STEP achieves the best average exact match and F1 scores across five benchmarks. The code, models, and training data are publicly available for further research and development.

entry.title: Researchers audit reproducibility of knowledge graph extraction from threat reports, finding variability in triple-F1 scores due to matching protocols and releasing CTIForge for standardized validation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers conducted a reproducibility audit of knowledge graph extraction tools used for threat reports, revealing that published triple-F1 scores vary significantly depending on how predicted triples are matched to gold annotations. They reimplemented matching rules for only five of twelve systems and found that rescoring under different protocols reversed many pairwise system rankings, with one prediction set's F1 score ranging from 0.16 to 0.70. Mechanical matchers agreed with multi-reviewer adjudication up to 71%, while a large language model judge reached 86% agreement. To isolate the effects of validation from extraction, the team developed CTIForge, a pipeline with a deterministic validation layer that can be varied independently of extraction outputs. Testing seven deployment configurations showed that validation increased precision for hosted backbones but decreased it for offline backbones, coinciding with more frequent disputes over entity types. The researchers released their pipeline, protocol suite, and detailed audit records to support further evaluation and standardization in this area.

entry.title: CliffRank introduces a dual-branch framework combining regression and ranking-consistency learning for activity-cliff prediction, achieving top Spearman correlations on antimicrobial peptide and small-molecule datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: CliffRank addresses the challenge of predicting activity cliffs, where small structural changes cause large activity differences, by training two parallel predictors using mean squared error, thresholded listwise loss, and Pairwise Preference Consistency (PPC). The method achieved the highest mean Spearman correlations on three antimicrobial peptide datasets with ESM2-t12 and on three small-molecule datasets with PNA, demonstrating improved ranking performance compared to existing methods. The study also explored the effects of asymmetric initialization and delayed activation of PPC, finding that these adjustments improved some metrics but did not universally enhance performance across all targets. The authors suggest future work to evaluate more targets, develop adaptive PPC schedules, and incorporate protein or membrane context to further improve activity-cliff ranking predictions.

entry.title: RecKAN introduces a learnable recursive polynomial basis for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, outperforming fixed-basis KANs on multiple classification and forecasting benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: RecKAN enhances Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks by learning the polynomial basis itself through a second-order polynomial recurrence with five coefficients trained jointly with the network. This approach generalizes classical polynomial families and allows the basis to adapt beyond fixed classical choices. Across diverse datasets including image, text, biomedical time series classification, and forecasting, RecKAN outperforms parameter-matched KAN baselines and achieves lower error rates, also improving accuracy when used as a classifier head with convolutional backbones on standard image datasets. The learned recurrence coefficients are interpretable and adapt to task-specific structural requirements, consistent with theoretical analysis.

entry.title: Researchers introduce VakyArth, the first pragmatic benchmark for Indic languages evaluating Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Malayalam across five linguistic phenomena [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: VakyArth is a new diagnostic benchmark designed to assess pragmatic competence in large language models (LLMs) across four Indic languages: Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Malayalam. It tests models on deixis, speech acts, implicature, social pragmatics, and coherence using multiple-choice questions, natural language inference, and translation tasks, with all items created by native speakers. The study finds consistent failures in LLMs when interpreting pragmatic meanings tied to Indic linguistic and cultural contexts, with notable differences in performance across languages and task types.

entry.title: hLLM introduces single-pass decoding for generative reranking using the Hungarian algorithm to achieve 64× speed-up with maintained ranking quality [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present hLLM, a decoding strategy for large language models that outputs ranked items in a single pass by treating the problem as a bipartite assignment solved via the Hungarian algorithm. This approach replaces traditional autoregressive decoding, which requires sequential passes per token, with an efficient method that decodes all ordinal values simultaneously. The team demonstrates that combining LoRA-based fine-tuning with teacher ranking distillation yields end-to-end inference in 28 milliseconds, achieving a 64-fold speed increase without sacrificing ranking accuracy. Their study includes a detailed analysis of architecture, training signals, and backbone adaptation, linking generative ranking to combinatorial optimization and suggesting potential for other constant-time decoding methods in real-time ranking applications.

entry.title: Import What You Need: Learning When and How to Augment EHR Graphs with External Knowledge [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.01839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Longitudinal prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) is limited by the sparsity and irregularity in patient trajectories, and knowledge augmentation with external knowledge graphs (KGs) offers a promising way to alleviate these issues. However, most existing methods perform fixed, context-agnostic topology augmentation by adding the same KG nodes and edges regardless of a patient's evolving state. We propose ReTA, a Reinforcement learning-based dynamic Topology Augmentation framework that casts KG import as a per-visit, budget-aware policy. ReTA first constructs an offline refined pool of KG-grounded templates, then learns a policy to select one augment action per visit from three options: Soft Import, which enriches node features without modifying graph topology, Hard Import, which grafts a compact KG subgraph onto the visit graph to create message-passing shortcuts, and Skip, which leaves the visit unaugmented when the base encoder is already confident. To stabilize learning, ReTA employs a decoupled encoder that processes semantic and structural signals in separate channels and fuses them via adaptive gating. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV across diagnosis prediction, mortality, and readmission show that ReTA consistently outperforms strong baselines while remaining efficient, transfers across datasets and knowledge graphs, and yields interpretable augmentation patterns. The robust gains under sparse supervision highlight the advantage of ReTA's dynamic decision to import knowledge, boosting accuracy while curbing costs.

entry.title: Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.01867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A major question in cognitive modeling concerns the behavioral alignment between large language models and humans across linguistic and non-linguistic tasks. Unlike standard LLMs, large reasoning models (LRMs) are optimized with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, encouraging correct solutions to reasoning tasks rather than preference-aligned responses. Recent work (de Varda et al., 2025) investigates the cost of thinking in humans and LRMs by comparing human reaction times with model reasoning traces across a range of reasoning tasks. We isolate this alignment by turning to abductive reasoning: unlike deductive tasks, its difficulty cannot be inferred from formal structure and offers no shortcuts a model could exploit to mimic effort without genuine search, providing firmer ground for empirical claims of shared effort. We find further evidence of alignment between LRM and human reasoning effort, as well as evidence that models and humans tend to make similar errors. Finally, we show that decoding methods that let models explore multiple reasoning paths increase alignment in reasoning cost between humans and LRMs across the three models tested.

entry.title: OutageDiT: A Generative Foundation Model for Power Outage Forecasting and Scenario Simulation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.01896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power-outage planning requires scenarios before an event occurs. These scenarios must represent uncertainty in magnitude, timing, and duration while preserving temporal dependence. However, severe events are rare, and data from any single region contain few examples of extreme outage and restoration patterns. To address this challenge, we introduce OutageDiT, a foundation model for generating seven-day outage trajectories at quarter-hour resolution, trained on outage and weather records across the United States. Specifically, a condition encoder processes the historical context and known future covariates once per forecast, and a shallow flow decoder reuses the resulting horizon-aligned states to generate complete trajectories. The resulting samples support point forecasting, uncertainty quantification, and conditional event simulation within one deep generative model. Across outage forecasting benchmarks, OutageDiT improves forecast accuracy and scenario quality over strong baselines and supports zero-shot transfer to held-out regions. Together, these results position conditional outage simulation as a bridge from outage forecasting to operational planning under uncertainty.

entry.title: Accurate in space, unreliable in time: how LLMs represent national cultural change [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.01902v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assessments of cultural alignment have become an important part of the development and improvement of large language models (LLMs). However, the majority of the evaluations treat culture as a single snapshot, investigating only whether a model represents a society accurately at the current time. Research in cultural psychology shows that cultural values change at different rates and directions over time. Therefore, a "culturally aware" model should capture not only where a culture is today but also how it has changed over time. We examine this missing dimension of cultural awareness using more than two decades of the World Values Survey data. We compare the cultural trajectories of 40 countries with the trajectories produced by four state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs on the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map. Our findings show that while models generally place countries close to their most recent surveyed positions, these representations tend to lag several years behind that position. They also capture only part of the magnitude of the observed change, introduce movement where little occurred, and rarely reproduce reversals in countries' trajectories. These findings point to temporal flattening and suggest that snapshot accuracy can give an incomplete picture of cultural awareness in LLMs and have implications for model evaluation, representational harms, and the governance of culturally aware AI systems.

entry.title: On-Policy Distillation Meets Off-Policy GRPO: Training Compact Instruction-Following Rerankers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.01947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compact instruction-following rerankers are attractive for deployment, but conventional distillation pipelines typically train students by offline imitation of teacher outputs on a fixed set of examples, constraining supervision to the teacher's observed ranking space. We revisit reranker distillation through the lens of reinforcement learning. We propose a two-stage framework combining off-policy teacher optimization with on-policy student distillation. In Stage 1, a 4B teacher reranker is strengthened with off-policy GRPO using LLM-judge feedback on 88K instruction-following examples. In Stage 2, a compact 1B student samples rankings from its own policy and receives soft teacher-derived rewards on those rankings, coupling student exploration with knowledge transfer. Our strongest gains appear under distribution shift. On MAIR-11, the original 11-subset, 869-query evaluation, the proposed student reaches 0.7670 nDCG@6, outperforming offline listwise KD by +4.6 points. Controlled comparisons against offline pairwise RankNet KD and on-policy GKD show that neither changing the offline distillation objective nor moving teacher-distribution matching on-policy reproduces the performance of reward-based on-policy distillation over student-sampled rankings. The advantage persists on MAIR-Full: across all 126 tasks and 9,356 queries, the proposed method obtains the highest task-macro point estimates among the evaluated distillation variants, reaching 0.6808 nDCG@6 and 0.7865 MRR@6. It also exceeds two released 7B RL-trained rerankers on the comparable MAIR-11 evaluation, while the same Stage 2 training procedure consistently improves three architecturally distinct alternative student backbones. On the 9,861-query validation benchmark, the resulting 1B reranker achieves 0.7624 nDCG@6 while providing a favorable quality-efficiency tradeoff relative to larger alternatives.

entry.title: Convergence Theory of Knowledge Distillation in Asynchronous P2P Gossip Learning Network [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.01952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decentralized, serverless learning increasingly connects devices running different architectures, where the standard tool, decentralized SGD, is undefined as models with different parameter counts cannot be averaged. Knowledge distillation (KD) exchanges soft predictions rather than weights and sidesteps this obstacle, yet convergence theory for fully decentralized, asynchronous peer-to-peer (P2P) KD is lacking. We provide one, relocating consensus from parameter space to function (output) space: a KD event is a geometric contraction operator in logit space on the peers' predictive distributions, which we analyse in the Hilbert space of predictions on a reference measure. Under standard smoothness/variance assumptions and two realizability assumptions, one bridging parameter SGD to the functional step and one controlling restricted task/KD alignment, the time-averaged functional stationarity and function-space disagreement converge at rate $O(1/(\eta T))$ to an $O(\eta)+O(B_f^2)+O(\zeta_f^2)$ neighbourhood. Here $B_f$ is the distance from the task optimum to the peers' reachable classes and $\zeta_f$ measures persistent local-task heterogeneity. Across homogeneous, width-heterogeneous, and mixed-family networks of the experiments, KD contracts function disagreement by $40-61\times$, while isolated training does not. The sampled stationarity diagnostic has late transient exponents $0.99-1.90$ on the shared-skeleton main runs, and the four-point step-size sweep exhibits the predicted transient: neighbourhood tradeoff.

entry.title: Transfer Safety Awareness for Cross-Modal Safety Drift in Multimodal Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02082v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual modality enhances the capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) but also introduces a safety concern: a benign textual query may convey harmful intent when grounded in a visual image. We term this cross-modal safety drift and our pilot studies show that the safety response rate for such requests is substantially lower than that for requests containing explicitly unsafe text. This paper aims to systematically study this issue. First, we conduct an empirical analysis to identify representative unsafe response patterns. Building on these, we interpret model representations and attentions, revealing that visually risky cues receive limited attention and weakly trigger refusal. Motivated by the observation that safety signals from unsafe text processing can be transferred, we propose safety-awareness representation transfer (SRT), a lightweight direction-refinement method that mitigates cross-modal safety drift with a frozen MLLM backbone. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and models show that SRT effectively improves safety in diverse cross-modal settings while preserving utility. Code is available at https://github.com/cucu220123/safety-awareness.

entry.title: Federated LoRA Adaptation of BiomedCLIP Across Four International Chest X-Ray Cohorts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets institutions train a shared model without exchanging data, and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) makes this practical at scale by communicating only compact low-rank updates. Biomedical imaging is a compelling setting for this combination: patient data are archived behind privacy regulations, and institutions differ widely in scanners, protocols, and compute. Such heterogeneity raises the question of how federated LoRA updates should be aggregated, increasingly pressing as multimodal vision-language models become central to medical image analysis. We benchmark federated Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of BiomedCLIP for chest radiograph classification across four public cohorts on three continents (USA, Vietnam, Spain). Federated LoRA adaptation improves shared-class AUC on all four cohorts over the unadapted BiomedCLIP backbone (mean 0.687 to 0.802), showing that the gains come from federated adaptation rather than from the pretrained model's zero-shot ability. Relative to isolated single-cohort training, federation improves the weaker cohorts while largely preserving the strongest and approaches a centralized reference (0.812) that pools all data. The singular value decomposition (SVD)-based product-space aggregation introduced by FlexLoRA is essential to this gain (naive factor averaging drops mean AUC by 0.097), whereas a drift-correcting optimizer (FedProx) shows no benefit over FedAvg in our single-seed runs, consistent with LoRA's low-rank updates already limiting client drift. Biomedical vision-language models can thus be adapted collaboratively across heterogeneous, geographically distributed institutions without centralizing data.

entry.title: Predict, Don't Iterate: Efficient Adaptive-Length Infilling for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to the auto-regressive paradigm. With bidirectional attention and any-order generation, DLMs naturally fit infilling tasks, which require generating a middle span conditioned on both the prefix and the suffix. However, infilling is sensitive to the length of the span, while DLMs require the length to be fixed before generation. Although prior studies extend DLMs to dynamic lengths, they still suffer from two limitations. (i) Sensitivity to initial length. These methods require a preset length to initialize the search and are highly sensitive to this initial length, often yielding suboptimal results. (ii) Inference inefficiency. They either insert length-changing operations during generation or repeatedly search for an appropriate length using multi-step denoising confidence, both of which introduce substantial extra forward passes and computational cost. Therefore, we propose PILL (Probing-based InfiLling with preset-Length-free decoding), an efficient infilling method for DLMs that requires no preset initial length and adds far fewer extra forward passes than baselines, substantially reducing inference time. Experiments show that, across five DLMs spanning different families, architectures, and training recipes on eight infilling benchmarks, PILL improves over the strongest baseline by +4.8 average pass rate on code and +6.0 BLEU-2 on text, while running 1.82x faster than that baseline. The code is available at https://github.com/Hsu1023/PILL.

entry.title: Disease Burden over Skin Tone: Decomposing the Dermatology-AI Generalization Gap [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02111v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dermatology artificial intelligence (AI) models are predominantly trained on light-skinned, cancer-focused image collections, yet they are increasingly proposed for deployment in resource-constrained settings where patients differ from training populations along two confounded axes: skin tone and disease distribution. We investigate whether poor generalization is primarily caused by skin-tone underrepresentation or disease-distribution shift. We evaluate a cancer-trained baseline (ResNet-50 fine-tuned on HAM10000 and ISIC 2019), two dermatology foundation models (DermLIP and MONET), and a general-purpose vision model (DINOv3) as frozen feature extractors. Models are evaluated on a tone-stratified disease-matched dataset (Diverse Dermatology Images, DDI) and a disease-shifted tone-diverse dataset (Skin Condition Image Network, SCIN). Our results show that disease-distribution shift contributes more than skin tone in the evaluated settings. The cancer baseline decreases from 0.62 to 0.21 balanced accuracy when transferred to unfamiliar clinical conditions, while the within-disease skin-tone gap is smaller (0.10-0.18) and inconsistent. Label-free representation analysis shows that this failure reflects a representational limitation rather than only missing output labels: cancer-specialized features poorly cluster unfamiliar conditions (kNN purity lift +0.06 over chance), whereas dermatology-pretrained features retain stronger transferable structure (+0.23). Finally, we show that representation quality predicts recoverable performance under lightweight adaptation. Starting from dermatology foundation models, approximately ten labeled examples per clinical category recover most attainable performance. We release the evaluation protocol and code to support reproducible auditing of dermatology AI generalization.

entry.title: text2ql: Multi-Target Natural Language Querying via a Language-Agnostic Intermediate Representation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural language interfaces to databases have traditionally suffered from three structural limitations: exclusive targeting of relational SQL, unconditional dependence on large language model (LLM) inference at query time, and absence of any runtime signal when generated queries are semantically incorrect. This paper presents text2ql, an open-source Python framework that addresses all three limitations through a language-agnostic Intermediate Representation (QueryIR) and a pluggable renderer architecture. A single seven-stage detection pipeline serves both SQL and GraphQL targets; a zero-LLM deterministic mode delivers 100% execution accuracy at a median latency of 3.2 ms with no API cost; and every generated query carries a runtime confidence score in [0.15, 0.97] computed from an additive signal model. Evaluated on 50-query random samples from the Spider and BIRD benchmarks (indicative results; full-set evaluation is planned), the LLM-backed mode achieves 62-70% exact match and 84-91% execution accuracy; the deterministic mode achieves 100% execution accuracy with zero parse errors across all 100 test cases. An ablation study isolates schema-aware prompting as the dominant accuracy lever, contributing +18.4 percentage points of exact-match gain over the schema-free baseline on both benchmarks. text2ql is publicly available at https://pypi.org/project/text2ql/ under the Apache 2.0 license.

entry.title: C$^{3}$T: Counterfactual Causal Reasoning for Sentiment Shifts in Social-Media Conversation Trees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sentiment in social-media threads does not only vary across posts; it shifts as users react to claims, corrections, evidence, and hostility within a branching reply tree. We study why sentiment changes in rumor-centric conversation trees by treating discourse moves (e.g., denial/correction, evidence/link, toxicity/attack) as candidate interventions and asking (i) what sentiment a reply expresses, (ii) whether the sentiment shifts relative to its parent, and (iii) which prior message most plausibly drove the reply's sentiment. To support this setting, we introduce CaSiRe, a causal sentiment reasoning layer over public rumor conversation datasets that adds post-level sentiment labels, induced parent-child shift labels, calibrated multi-label intervention tags, and explicitly annotated causal-source labels. We then propose C$^{3}$T (Counterfactual Causal Conversation Transformer), a thread-structured temporal model that jointly predicts node sentiment and shifts, learns sparse ancestor attribution, and supports counterfactual queries by forcing conversational intervention embeddings on or off to estimate potential outcomes. Under an event-level split, C$^{3}$T improves out-of-event robustness and attribution over text-only, graph-based, and temporal baselines, and yields interpretable model-based effects: denials/corrections and evidence reduce downstream negativity, while toxicity increases it. We also benchmark open-weight LLM prompting baselines and find that added conversational context helps, but attribution remains less reliable, motivating structure-aware counterfactual modeling for social-media analysis.

entry.title: A Power Law in Logarithm's Clothing: On the Scalability of Graph-Based Vector Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02143v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Most vector databases rely on graph-based indexes, notably HNSW and Vamana, for approximate nearest neighbor search. entry.title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Matching the Offline $0.401$ Factor [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed subsets of the $d$-dimensional unit cube. The best known constructive offline approximation factor is $0.401$ under the corresponding meta-solvability assumptions, whereas comparable adversarial online guarantees had remained at $1/e$. We show that this factor is also achievable online. In the post-decision full-information value-oracle model, our algorithm attains factor $0.401$ with sublinear approximate regret when oracle feedback is conditionally unbiased and bounded. The online algorithm does not run the offline construction on a changing objective. Instead, it replaces the offline objective-dependent box step by a weighted online learner that controls the required residual terms cumulatively. An exact asymmetric balance theorem preserves the offline coefficients despite adversarial variation. The direct implementation has $O(T^{3/4})$ regret and uses $O(dT^{1/4})$ oracle calls per round. More generally, for every $\delta\in[0,1/4]$, batching gives $O(T^\delta)$ calls per round and $O(T^{4/5-\delta/5})$ regret, including a one-call $O(T^{4/5})$ endpoint. Under a positive-anchor condition, randomized blocking retains factor $0.401$ with $O(T^{5/6})$ one-point bandit regret.

entry.title: OBJECTION! Lawyer Agents Mitigate Guilty Bias in Legal Judgment Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP) models are typically trained on documents that describe facts from a prosecutorial perspective. Existing datasets further exhibit severe label imbalance toward guilty outcomes. Consequently, these models suffer from "Guilty Bias", blindly accepting the prosecution's narrative as objective truth. Previous studies employing three-step reasoning structures or training on synthetically generated innocence data improve overall accuracy, but they still fail to mitigate bias at inference time. In this paper, we introduce OBJECTION, an inference-time pipeline that integrates an Adversarial Lawyer Agent into each 3-step reasoning of offense, unlawfulness, and culpability. Unlike generic critics, our agent actively challenges the model's presumptions of guilt by injecting legal defense arguments at each reasoning stage. To thoroughly evaluate this, we present a new "Natural Innocent" dataset including 3.4k real-world cases, overcoming the limitations of synthetic innocence benchmarks. Test results show that OBJECTION drastically reduces the False Guilty Rate (FGR) from 82.93% (SOTA baseline) to 16.69%, proving its capability to perform substantive legal reasoning. This work denotes a key progress toward aligning Legal AI with the presumption of innocence.

entry.title: GeoSPRINT: Geometric Redundancy-Aware Step Pruning for Inference in Diffusion Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models achieve high sample quality but remain expensive at inference time because sampling requires many sequential neural function evaluations (NFEs). Existing acceleration methods either use fixed step-skipping schedules, adapt step sizes based on local numerical error, or require additional training. We introduce GeoSPRINT (Geometric Step Pruning for Inference in Trajectories), a training-free framework for constructing non-uniform sampling schedules from the geometry of denoising trajectories. GeoSPRINT detects geometrically redundant steps using a hyperplanarity test in latent space, implemented efficiently via QR factorization, and converts the resulting redundancy profile into a sampling schedule that allocates more steps to high-curvature regions of the trajectory. In addition, we introduce the trajectory projection score $\alpha_{\mathrm{traj}}$, a residual-variance metric that quantifies trajectory straightness and serves as a model-free diagnostic for rectified flow quality. Across CIFAR-10 ($32{\times}32$), LSUN Church ($256{\times}256$), and Stable Diffusion v1.5 ($512{\times}512$ latent), GeoSPRINT consistently improves over uniform DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models) schedules at matched NFE budgets. On CIFAR-10, GeoSPRINT improves FID (Fr\'echet Inception Distance) by 0.7-1.1 over DDIM across 49-89 NFEs and surpasses DPM-Solver++ at NFE${\geq}30$ despite using a first-order DDIM solver. On LSUN Church, it reduces FID from 1.48 to 1.26 at 52 steps, and on Stable Diffusion v1.5 it achieves up to 1.93 FID improvement over DDIM. These results show that trajectory geometry provides a useful global signal for allocating inference steps and that schedule quality can substantially improve diffusion sampling efficiency without retraining.

entry.title: Schr\"odinger Bridges on Lie Group Manifolds for Probabilistic Intrinsic Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02196v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative modeling directly on geometric manifolds can avoid errors introduced by flattening non-Euclidean data, repeated ambient projection, and coordinate inconsistency in Euclidean representations. Schrodinger bridges provide a probabilistic generative framework for entropy-regularized transport between prescribed endpoint distributions. We study Schrodinger bridges for kinetic dynamics on Lie group manifolds with state X_t = (g_t, xi_t) in G x g, allowing endpoint observations to constrain only the variables that are actually measured. In particular, the entropy projection determines the conditional law of the unobserved endpoint velocities. For the same observed endpoint bridge, we develop two computational realizations: Wrapped-Kernel Bridge Calibration (WKBC) uses an explicit periodized kinetic kernel on compact Abelian groups, whereas Reciprocal Conditional-Control Bridge Matching (RCCBM) handles compact non-Abelian groups through two-sided endpoint calibration and mollified conditional-control matching. The canonical teacher-mixture path law is itself a Markov reciprocal law, so forward generation uses a calibrated initial law and one learned Doob controller. Moreover, we establish a modular error bound in the bounded-Lipschitz path metric that provides a clean separation of errors due to endpoints, control regression, initialization, discretization, and related approximations. Experiments on multiple Lie group manifold datasets validate the feasibility and consistency of our proposed method, covering protein and RNA torsions, SO(3), U(n), and the Protein Conformational Transition Pathway Generation task using mdCATH trajectories in a compact reduced representation. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/cafferyzhang12/Schr-dinger_Bridge_on_LieGroup.

entry.title: SMart: A Multi-source Multi-phase Time Series Representation Transfer Framework [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2609.02203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time series representation learning (TSRL) has attracted growing research interests in recent years. Two recent explorations in TSRL are: i) exploiting a transformer-based framework to learn time series; ii) instead of using only the targeted dataset, borrowing time series from other datasets to to facilitate representation transfer. While these two explorations are shown effective, the self-supervised time series recovery task in (i) and the single-source dataset used in (ii) are technically simple and thus can be enhanced with new ideas.
